title: Ἀχιλλεὺς ἐν Τρώεσσιν
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Hera answers Poseidon: let him decide for himself whether to save Aeneas, since she and Athena have sworn never to defend the Trojans, not even when all Troy burns. Poseidon goes into the fighting, pours a haze over Achilles’ eyes, draws the spear out of Aeneas’ shield, lifts Aeneas over the ranks of men and horses and sets him down at the edge of the war. He tells him to give way whenever he meets Achilles, but to fight among the foremost once Achilles is dead, since no other Achaean will kill him. Poseidon clears the haze, and Achilles, seeing his spear on the ground and no man to aim it at, decides that Aeneas was dear to the gods after all, lets him go, and goes down the ranks urging the Achaeans to fight man against man. Hector calls to the Trojans not to fear Achilles; the armies close. Apollo stands beside Hector and tells him to keep out of Achilles’ way, and Hector shrinks back into the crowd. Achilles kills Iphition, the son of a water-nymph, and taunts him with his far-off home; he kills Demoleon through the helmet and Hippodamas, who bellows like a bull dragged about by youths, to the delight of the earth-shaker. Last he overtakes Polydorus, Priam’s youngest son, whom his father had forbidden to fight and who was showing off his speed; Achilles’ javelin strikes him in the back where the belt meets the breastplate and comes out at the navel, and he falls to his knees holding in his entrails.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita boōpis potnia Hērē·
sentences.l: Him then answered ox-eyed lady Hera:
sentences.i: Then ox-eyed lady Hera answered him:
sentences.n: A reply-formula: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ‘him then answered’, with ἠμείβετ’ the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’. τόν is ‘him’, Poseidon, whose speech ended at 308. βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη ‘ox-eyed lady Hera’ is a stock epithet, translated every time; the usual explanation is large, calm eyes. The paragraph break marks the change of speaker.

sentences.t:
ἐννοσίγαι’, αὐτὸς σὺ μετὰ φρεσὶ σῇσι νόησον
Αἰνείαν ἤ κέν μιν ἐρύσσεαι ἦ κεν ἐάσῃς
Πηλεΐδῃ Ἀχιλῆϊ δαμήμεναι, ἐσθλὸν ἐόντα.
sentences.tr:
ennosigai’, autos sy meta phresi sēisi noēson
Aineian ē ken min erysseai ē ken easēis
Pēleïdēi Achilēï damēmenai, esthlon eonta.
sentences.l:
“Earth-shaker, you yourself in your own wits consider
Aeneas, whether you will draw him out or allow
him to be subdued by Peleus’-son Achilles, though he is good.
sentences.i: “Earth-shaker, consider in your own wits whether you will rescue Aeneas or let him be overcome by Peleus’ son Achilles, good as he is.
sentences.n: ἐννοσίγαι’ is the vocative of ἐννοσίγαιος ‘earth-shaker’, elided before αὐτός; the epithet stands for Poseidon’s name. νόησον is the aorist imperative of νοέω ‘consider’. Αἰνείαν is the object of νόησον and is put first; μιν then takes it up as the object of ἐρύσσεαι: ἤ κεν … ἐρύσσεαι ἦ κεν ἐάσῃς ‘whether you will draw … out or allow’. ἐρύσσεαι is from ἐρύομαι ‘draw out’ (‘rescue’ in i; with κεν, a subjunctive), ἐάσῃς the aorist subjunctive of ἐάω ‘allow’. δαμήμεναι is the aorist passive infinitive of δάμνημι ‘subdue’, with the dative Πηλεΐδῃ Ἀχιλῆϊ ‘by Peleus’ son Achilles’. The accusative subject of δαμήμεναι is Aeneas again, understood from μιν; ἐσθλὸν ἐόντα ‘being good’ is accusative, agreeing with him.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι μὲν γὰρ νῶϊ πολέας ὠμόσσαμεν ὅρκους
πᾶσι μετ’ ἀθανάτοισιν ἐγὼ καὶ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη
μή ποτ’ ἐπὶ Τρώεσσιν ἀλεξήσειν κακὸν ἦμαρ,
sentences.tr:
ētoi men gar nōï poleas ōmossamen horkous
pasi met’ athanatoisin egō kai Pallas Athēnē
mē pot’ epi Trōessin alexēsein kakon ēmar,
sentences.l:
For truly we two have sworn many oaths
among all the immortals, I and Pallas Athena,
never for the Trojans to ward off the evil day,
sentences.i: For we two have sworn many oaths among all the immortals, Pallas Athena and I, never to ward off the evil day for the Trojans,
sentences.n: ἤτοι μὲν γάρ ‘for truly’, with ἤτοι printed as one word. νῶϊ is the dual ‘we two’, which ἐγὼ καὶ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη explains. ὠμόσσαμεν is the aorist of ὄμνυμι ‘swear’; πολέας is the epic accusative plural of πολύς. The oath is told with an infinitive: μή ποτ’ … ἀλεξήσειν, future infinitive of ἀλέξω ‘ward off’, with κακὸν ἦμαρ ‘the evil day’ and the dative Τρώεσσιν ‘for the Trojans’ (ἐπί goes with it). The sentence is cut at the comma because it runs on for five lines.

sentences.t:
μηδ’ ὁπότ’ ἂν Τροίη μαλερῷ πυρὶ πᾶσα δάηται
καιομένη, καίωσι δ’ ἀρήϊοι υἷες Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
mēd’ hopot’ an Troiē malerōi pyri pasa daētai
kaiomenē, kaiōsi d’ arēïoi huies Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
nor when Troy with devouring fire is all burnt,
burning, and burn it the warlike sons of the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: nor even when all Troy is burnt with devouring fire, burning, and the warlike sons of the Achaeans burn it.”
sentences.n: μηδ’ ‘nor’ continues the oath. ὁπότ’ ἂν … δάηται ‘whenever … is burnt’ is an aorist passive subjunctive of δαίω ‘burn’. Τροίη … πᾶσα ‘all Troy’ has the epic ending -η. μαλερῷ πυρί ‘with devouring fire’: μαλερός ‘devouring’ is a traditional gloss. καιομένη ‘burning’ agrees with Τροίη; καίωσι is a present subjunctive ‘they burn (it)’, its subject ἀρήϊοι υἷες Ἀχαιῶν ‘the warlike sons of the Achaeans’ (υἷες = υἱοί). Hera’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ τό γ’ ἄκουσε Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων,
βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν ἄν τε μάχην καὶ ἀνὰ κλόνον ἐγχειάων,
ἷξε δ’ ὅθ’ Αἰνείας ἠδ’ ὃ κλυτὸς ἦεν Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.tr:
autar epei to g’ akouse Poseidaōn enosichthōn,
bē rh’ imen an te machēn kai ana klonon encheiaōn,
hixe d’ hoth’ Aineias ēd’ ho klytos ēen Achilleus.
sentences.l:
But when that he heard, Poseidon earth-shaker,
he set out to go through the battle and through the turmoil of spears,
and came to where Aeneas was, and famous Achilles too.
sentences.i: But when Poseidon earth-shaker heard that, he set out through the battle and the turmoil of spears, and came to where Aeneas was, and famous Achilles.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ‘but when’ takes the aorist ἄκουσε ‘heard’ (ἀκούω); τό γ’ ‘that’ is Hera’s speech. ἐνοσίχθων is translated ‘earth-shaker’ every time. βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν ‘set out to go’: βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω without augment, ἴμεν the epic infinitive of εἶμι. ἄν τε is ἀνά τε, ‘through … and through’ with the accusatives μάχην and κλόνον; ἐγχειάων is the epic genitive plural of ἐγχείη ‘spear’. ἷξε is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘came’. ἠδ’ ὃ κλυτὸς … Ἀχιλλεύς ‘and famous Achilles’ is a second subject of ἦεν (the epic imperfect of εἰμί, singular as the nearer subject). The paragraph break marks Poseidon’s move.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα τῷ μὲν ἔπειτα κατ’ ὀφθαλμῶν χέεν ἀχλὺν
Πηλεΐδῃ Ἀχιλῆϊ· ὃ δὲ μελίην εὔχαλκον
ἀσπίδος ἐξέρυσεν μεγαλήτορος Αἰνείαο·
sentences.tr:
autika tōi men epeita kat’ ophthalmōn cheen achlyn
Pēleïdēi Achilēï· ho de meliēn euchalkon
aspidos exerysen megalētoros Aineiao·
sentences.i: At once he poured a haze over the eyes of Peleus’ son Achilles; and he drew the ash-spear of good bronze out of the shield of great-spirited Aeneas;
sentences.n: αὐτίκα ‘at once’. τῷ μέν … Πηλεΐδῃ Ἀχιλῆϊ ‘for the one … for Peleus’ son Achilles’: the dative says whose eyes are covered, and is then named. κατ’ ὀφθαλμῶν ‘over his eyes’, χέεν the aorist of χέω ‘pour’, ἀχλύν ‘haze’. Poseidon is the unnamed subject; ὃ δέ ‘and he’ takes up the same man. μελίην ‘ash-spear’; εὔχαλκον is εὖ + χαλκός, ‘of good bronze’. ἐξέρυσεν is the aorist of ἐξερύω ‘draw out’; ἀσπίδος … Αἰνείαο ‘out of the shield of Aeneas’; μεγαλήτορος ‘great-spirited’ is a stock epithet.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὴν μὲν προπάροιθε ποδῶν Ἀχιλῆος ἔθηκεν,
Αἰνείαν δ’ ἔσσευεν ἀπὸ χθονὸς ὑψόσ’ ἀείρας.
sentences.tr:
kai tēn men proparoithe podōn Achilēos ethēken,
Aineian d’ esseuen apo chthonos hypsos’ aeiras.
sentences.l:
and it, on the one hand, before the feet of Achilles he set,
but Aeneas he sent rushing from the ground, lifting him high.
sentences.i: and set the spear down before the feet of Achilles, but he lifted Aeneas high from the ground and sent him speeding away.
sentences.n: τὴν μέν … Αἰνείαν δέ ‘it, on the one hand … Aeneas, on the other’; τήν is the spear (μελίην, feminine). προπάροιθε ποδῶν ‘before the feet’ takes the genitive; ἔθηκεν is the aorist of τίθημι ‘set’. ἔσσευεν is the aorist of σεύω ‘set rushing’ (with doubled σ); ἀείρας ‘lifting’; ὑψόσ’ ‘high up’ (ὑψόσε); ἀπὸ χθονός ‘from the ground’.

sentences.t:
πολλὰς δὲ στίχας ἡρώων, πολλὰς δὲ καὶ ἵππων
Αἰνείας ὑπερᾶλτο θεοῦ ἀπὸ χειρὸς ὀρούσας,
ἷξε δ’ ἐπ’ ἐσχατιὴν πολυάϊκος πολέμοιο,
ἔνθά τε Καύκωνες πόλεμον μέτα θωρήσσοντο.
sentences.tr:
pollas de stichas hērōōn, pollas de kai hippōn
Aineias hyperalto theou apo cheiros orousas,
hixe d’ ep’ eschatiēn polyaïkos polemoio,
entha te Kaukōnes polemon meta thōrēssonto.
sentences.l:
And many ranks of heroes, and many too of horses,
Aeneas leapt over, rushing from the god’s hand,
and came to the edge of much-rushing war,
where the Caucones were arming themselves for the war.
sentences.i: Aeneas leapt over many ranks of heroes and many of horses, rushing from the god’s hand, and came to the edge of onrushing war, where the Caucones were arming themselves for battle.
sentences.n: One sentence with Aeneas as the subject of two verbs: ὑπερᾶλτο, the aorist of ὑπεράλλομαι ‘leap over’ (with ὀρούσας ‘rushing, leaping’, from ὀρούω), and ἷξε ‘came’. πολλὰς … στίχας ‘many ranks’ is the object, with ἡρώων ‘of heroes’ and ἵππων ‘of horses’. θεοῦ ἀπὸ χειρός ‘from the god’s hand’. ἐσχατιή ‘the edge’. πολυάϊκος πολέμοιο ‘of onrushing war’: the sense of πολυάϊκος is not certain, and this is one traditional guess. Καύκωνες is the name of a people; only the name is given here. θωρήσσοντο is the imperfect middle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’; πόλεμον μέτα (μετά with the accusative, accent drawn back) ‘for the war’.

sentences.t:
τῷ δὲ μάλ’ ἐγγύθεν ἦλθε Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
tōi de mal’ engythen ēlthe Poseidaōn enosichthōn,
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
And to him, very near, came Poseidon earth-shaker,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Poseidon earth-shaker came very near to him, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: τῷ δέ ‘to him’ (Aeneas) goes with ἐγγύθεν ‘from close by’ and ἦλθε ‘came’ (aorist of ἔρχομαι). Line 331 is a stock speech introduction: μιν ‘him’, φωνήσας ‘lifting his voice’, ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’, προσηύδα ‘spoke to’ (imperfect of προσαυδάω). The line is the same wherever it stands, with μιν meaning whoever is addressed; here it is ‘him’. ἐνοσίχθων ‘earth-shaker’ again.

sentences.l:
“Aeneas, which of the gods thus you, reckless, orders
against the son of Peleus, the high-hearted, to fight,
who is at once stronger than you and dearer to the immortals?
sentences.i: “Aeneas, which of the gods tells you, reckless as you are, to fight against the high-hearted son of Peleus, who is both stronger than you and dearer to the immortals?
sentences.n: Αἰνεία is the vocative. τίς … θεῶν ‘which of the gods’; σ’ is σε ‘you’; ὧδε ‘thus’. ἀτέοντα ‘reckless’ is a rare participle, accusative, agreeing with σ’; it seems to belong to the family of ἄτη (‘bewilderment’ elsewhere in this text, which this verb need not share). Its exact sense is not certain, and ‘reckless’ is a guess from the context and the family. κελεύει ‘orders’ takes the infinitive μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’. ἀντία takes the genitive Πηλεΐωνος ‘of the son of Peleus’ (Achilles), with ὑπερθύμοιο, the epic genitive of ὑπέρθυμος ‘high-hearted’. ὃς σεῦ ἅμα κρείσσων καὶ φίλτερος: σεῦ is the epic genitive of σύ ‘than you’; ἅμα ‘at once’; κρείσσων ‘stronger’ and φίλτερος ‘dearer’ with the dative ἀθανάτοισιν. The Greek question mark ends the unit.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἀναχωρῆσαι ὅτε κεν συμβλήσεαι αὐτῷ,
μὴ καὶ ὑπὲρ μοῖραν δόμον Ἄϊδος εἰσαφίκηαι.
sentences.tr:
all’ anachōrēsai hote ken symblēseai autōi,
mē kai hyper moiran domon Aïdos eisaphikēai.
sentences.l:
But step back, whenever you meet him,
lest even beyond fate to the house of Hades you come.
sentences.i: But step back whenever you meet him, lest even beyond what is fated you come to the house of Hades.
sentences.n: ἀναχωρῆσαι is an aorist infinitive used as a command, ‘step back’ (ἀναχωρέω). ὅτε κεν συμβλήσεαι αὐτῷ ‘whenever you meet him’: the aorist subjunctive of συμβάλλομαι ‘meet’, with the epic ending -εαι for -ῃ. μὴ … εἰσαφίκηαι ‘lest you come’ is the aorist subjunctive of εἰσαφικνέομαι, with the epic ending -ηαι. ὑπὲρ μοῖραν ‘beyond fate’, δόμον Ἄϊδος ‘the house of Hades’; καί ‘even’ goes with ὑπὲρ μοῖραν.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί κ’ Ἀχιλεὺς θάνατον καὶ πότμον ἐπίσπῃ,
θαρσήσας δὴ ἔπειτα μετὰ πρώτοισι μάχεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
autar epei k’ Achileus thanaton kai potmon epispēi,
tharsēsas dē epeita meta prōtoisi machesthai·
sentences.l:
But when Achilles death and doom shall meet,
then take heart, indeed, and among the first fight;
sentences.i: But when Achilles has met his death and doom, then take heart and fight among the foremost;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί κ’ ‘but when’ is ἐπεί κε, which takes the aorist subjunctive ἐπίσπῃ (from ἐφέπω ‘come upon, meet’); θάνατον καὶ πότμον ‘death and doom’ are its objects. θαρσήσας … μάχεσθαι is the aorist participle of θαρσέω ‘take heart’ with the infinitive ‘to fight’, which here stands for a command, as ἀναχωρῆσαι did at 335. μετὰ πρώτοισι ‘among the first’; δὴ ἔπειτα ‘indeed then’.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γάρ τίς σ’ ἄλλος Ἀχαιῶν ἐξεναρίξει.
sentences.tr: ou men gar tis s’ allos Achaiōn exenarixei.
sentences.l: for not indeed will any other of the Achaeans despoil you.”
sentences.i: for no other of the Achaeans will kill you and strip you of your armour.”
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ ‘for truly not’. τίς … ἄλλος Ἀχαιῶν ‘any other of the Achaeans’. ἐξεναρίξει is the future of ἐξεναρίζω, which means to kill a man and strip him of his armour (from ἐνάρα ‘spoils’); i carries both halves, and l has ‘despoil’. The line gives the reason for taking heart after Achilles’ death. Poseidon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν λίπεν αὐτόθ’, ἐπεὶ διεπέφραδε πάντα.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn lipen autoth’, epei diepephrade panta.
sentences.l: So having spoken, he left him there, since he had made all things plain.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and left him there, since he had made everything plain.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’. λίπεν is the aorist of λείπω ‘left’, without augment; αὐτόθ’ is αὐτόθι ‘there, on the spot’. διεπέφραδε is an aorist of διαφράζω ‘explain, make plain’, with a reduplicated stem; ἐπεί here means ‘since’. πάντα ‘all things’. The paragraph break marks Poseidon’s departure.

sentences.t:
αἶψα δ’ ἔπειτ’ Ἀχιλῆος ἀπ’ ὀφθαλμῶν σκέδασ’ ἀχλὺν
θεσπεσίην·
sentences.tr:
aipsa d’ epeit’ Achilēos ap’ ophthalmōn skedas’ achlyn
thespesiēn·
sentences.l:
At once then from Achilles’ eyes he scattered the haze,
the wondrous one;
sentences.i: At once he scattered from Achilles’ eyes the wondrous haze;
sentences.n: αἶψα ‘at once’; ἀπ’ ὀφθαλμῶν ‘from the eyes’, with Ἀχιλῆος, the epic genitive of Ἀχιλλεύς. σκέδασ’ is the aorist of σκεδάννυμι ‘scatter’, elided. ἀχλύν ‘haze’ is the haze of 321, and θεσπεσίην ‘wondrous’ agrees with it. Poseidon is still the unnamed subject. The ano teleia ends the unit after θεσπεσίην.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἔπειτα μέγ’ ἔξιδεν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν,
ὀχθήσας δ’ ἄρα εἶπε πρὸς ὃν μεγαλήτορα θυμόν·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ epeita meg’ exiden ophthalmoisin,
ochthēsas d’ ara eipe pros hon megalētora thymon·
sentences.l:
and he then greatly saw out with his eyes,
and, vexed, he then spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.i: and then he looked hard with his eyes, and, troubled, spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Achilles. ἔξιδεν is the aorist of ἐξοράω, here ‘see out, look hard’, without augment; μέγ’ is an adverb ‘greatly’, and the exact force of the pair is not certain. Line 343 is a stock line: ὀχθήσας ‘vexed, troubled’ (aorist participle of ὀχθέω), εἶπε ‘spoke’, πρὸς ὃν … θυμόν ‘to his own heart’ (ὅς here is possessive), μεγαλήτορα ‘great-spirited’. The colon opens his words to himself.

sentences.t: ὢ πόποι ἦ μέγα θαῦμα τόδ’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ὁρῶμαι·
sentences.tr: ō popoi ē mega thauma tod’ ophthalmoisin horōmai·
sentences.l: “Ah, truly a great wonder this with my eyes I behold:
sentences.i: “Ah, this is truly a great wonder that I behold with my own eyes:
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is a cry of surprise, ‘ah’. ἦ ‘truly’; μέγα θαῦμα ‘a great wonder’; τόδ’ ‘this’. ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ‘with my eyes’ is the epic dative plural. ὁρῶμαι has a middle ending but the sense of the active ὁρῶ ‘I see, behold’. The colon points to what he sees, which the next lines give.

sentences.t:
ἔγχος μὲν τόδε κεῖται ἐπὶ χθονός, οὐδέ τι φῶτα
λεύσσω, τῷ ἐφέηκα κατακτάμεναι μενεαίνων.
sentences.tr:
enchos men tode keitai epi chthonos, oude ti phōta
leussō, tōi epheēka kataktamenai meneainōn.
sentences.l:
This spear, on the one hand, lies on the ground, and no man at all
I see, at whom I let it fly, eager to kill him.
sentences.i: This spear of mine lies on the ground, and I can see no man at all at whom I let it fly, eager as I was to kill him.
sentences.n: ἔγχος μὲν τόδε ‘this spear’: the μέν is answered by the οὐδέ clause. κεῖται ‘lies’, ἐπὶ χθονός ‘on the ground’. οὐδέ τι φῶτα λεύσσω ‘and I see no man at all’ (φώς ‘man’, λεύσσω ‘see’). τῷ ἐφέηκα ‘at whom I let it fly’: τῷ is a relative here (‘to whom’), ἐφέηκα the aorist of ἐφίημι ‘send at’. κατακτάμεναι is the aorist infinitive of κατακτείνω ‘to kill’, and μενεαίνων ‘being eager’ goes with the speaker.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα καὶ Αἰνείας φίλος ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσιν
ἦεν· ἀτάρ μιν ἔφην μὰψ αὔτως εὐχετάασθαι.
sentences.tr:
ē rha kai Aineias philos athanatoisi theoisin
ēen· atar min ephēn maps autōs euchetaasthai.
sentences.l:
Truly then even Aeneas was dear to the immortal gods;
but I said that he boasted, in vain, just so.
sentences.i: Truly, Aeneas too was dear to the immortal gods; and I thought he was boasting to no purpose.
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί ‘truly then, even’ (not the narrative ἦ ῥα καί ‘he spoke, and’): in speech ἦ ῥα marks a conclusion he has just reached. Αἰνείας … φίλος ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσιν ἦεν ‘Aeneas was dear to the immortal gods’ (φίλος with the dative; ἦεν is the epic imperfect of εἰμί). ἀτάρ ‘but, yet’. ἔφην is the imperfect of φημί ‘I said, I thought’, with μιν ‘him’ as subject of the infinitive εὐχετάασθαι, the uncontracted form of εὐχετάομαι ‘boast’ (here the sense of a vaunt, not ‘pray’). μὰψ αὔτως ‘in vain, just so’, that is, idly and with nothing behind it.

sentences.t: ἐρρέτω·
sentences.tr: erretō·
sentences.l: Let him go his way with ill luck;
sentences.i: Let him go, and ill luck go with him;
sentences.n: ἐρρέτω is the imperative of ἔρρω ‘go away with ill luck’, a dismissal that wishes him ill without saying that he will be destroyed. It is a unit of its own because the ano teleia follows it.

sentences.t:
οὔ οἱ θυμὸς ἐμεῦ ἔτι πειρηθῆναι
ἔσσεται, ὃς καὶ νῦν φύγεν ἄσμενος ἐκ θανάτοιο.
sentences.tr:
ou hoi thymos emeu eti peirēthēnai
essetai, hos kai nyn phygen asmenos ek thanatoio.
sentences.l:
not for him will there be heart to make trial of me again,
who even now escaped, glad, out of death.
sentences.i: He will not have the heart to make trial of me again, he who has even now escaped, glad, from death.
sentences.n: οὔ οἱ θυμὸς … ἔσσεται ‘he will not have the heart’: οἱ is the dative ‘to him’, θυμός ‘heart’, ἔσσεται the epic future of εἰμί. ἐμεῦ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ, taken by πειρηθῆναι, an aorist passive infinitive in the middle sense ‘make trial of’. ἔτι ‘again, any more’. ὃς καὶ νῦν ‘who even now’; φύγεν is the aorist of φεύγω without augment; ἄσμενος ‘glad’; ἐκ θανάτοιο ‘out of death’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ Δαναοῖσι φιλοπτολέμοισι κελεύσας
τῶν ἄλλων Τρώων πειρήσομαι ἀντίος ἐλθών.
sentences.tr:
all’ age dē Danaoisi philoptolemoisi keleusas
tōn allōn Trōōn peirēsomai antios elthōn.
sentences.l:
But come now, having bidden on the war-loving Danaans,
of the other Trojans I will make trial, having gone to meet them.”
sentences.i: But come now, I will call on the war-loving Danaans and make trial of the other Trojans, going to meet them.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή ‘but come now’. Δαναοῖσι φιλοπτολέμοισι ‘the war-loving Danaans’, datives taken by κελεύσας, the aorist participle of κελεύω ‘bid, order’ (‘bidden on’ in l, ‘call on’ in i). τῶν ἄλλων Τρώων ‘the other Trojans’ is genitive, taken by πειρήσομαι ‘I shall make trial of’. ἀντίος ἐλθών ‘having gone to meet them’ is the aorist participle of ἔρχομαι with ἀντίος ‘facing’. Achilles’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ἦ, καὶ ἐπὶ στίχας ἆλτο, κέλευε δὲ φωτὶ ἑκάστῳ·
sentences.tr: ē, kai epi stichas alto, keleue de phōti hekastōi·
sentences.l: He spoke, and along the ranks he leapt, and he ordered each man:
sentences.i: So he said, and sprang along the ranks, giving orders to each man:
sentences.n: ἦ is ‘he said’ (the old verb ἠμί), and καί joins what he did next. ἐπὶ στίχας ‘along the ranks’, ἆλτο the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leapt’. κέλευε is the imperfect of κελεύω ‘was ordering’, φωτὶ ἑκάστῳ ‘to each man’. The paragraph break marks a change from his words to the army: the colon opens a second speech, now to the Achaeans.

sentences.t:
μηκέτι νῦν Τρώων ἑκὰς ἕστατε δῖοι Ἀχαιοί,
ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ἀνὴρ ἄντ’ ἀνδρὸς ἴτω, μεμάτω δὲ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
mēketi nyn Trōōn hekas hestate dioi Achaioi,
all’ ag’ anēr ant’ andros itō, mematō de machesthai.
sentences.l:
“No longer now far from the Trojans stand, heavenly Achaeans,
but come, man against man let him go, and let him be eager to fight.
sentences.i: “Do not stand any longer far from the Trojans, heavenly Achaeans, but come, let man go against man, and let him be eager to fight.
sentences.n: μηκέτι νῦν ‘no longer now’ forbids with ἕστατε, the second plural perfect imperative of ἵστημι ‘stand’; Τρώων ἑκάς ‘far from the Trojans’ (ἑκάς takes the genitive). δῖοι ‘heavenly’ is the stock word, here of the Achaeans. ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ‘but come’; ἀνὴρ ἄντ’ ἀνδρὸς ἴτω ‘let man go against man’, with ἴτω the imperative of εἶμι; μεμάτω is the perfect imperative of μέμονα ‘be eager’, with the infinitive μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’.

sentences.t:
ἀργαλέον δέ μοί ἐστι καὶ ἰφθίμῳ περ ἐόντι
τοσσούσδ’ ἀνθρώπους ἐφέπειν καὶ πᾶσι μάχεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
argaleon de moi esti kai iphthimōi per eonti
tossousd’ anthrōpous ephepein kai pasi machesthai·
sentences.l:
And hard it is for me, even though I am mighty,
so many men to go against, and with all to fight;
sentences.i: It is hard for me, mighty as I am, to go against so many men and fight with them all;
sentences.n: ἀργαλέον … ἐστί ‘it is hard’ takes two infinitives: ἐφέπειν ‘go against’, with the accusative τοσσούσδ’ ἀνθρώπους ‘so many men’ (τοσσούσδε, with the suffix -δε), and μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ with πᾶσι ‘all’. καὶ ἰφθίμῳ περ ἐόντι ‘even though being mighty’ is dative, agreeing with μοί; ἴφθιμος ‘mighty’. The ano teleia ends the unit.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κ’ Ἄρης, ὅς περ θεὸς ἄμβροτος, οὐδέ κ’ Ἀθήνη
τοσσῆσδ’ ὑσμίνης ἐφέποι στόμα καὶ πονέοιτο·
sentences.tr:
oude k’ Arēs, hos per theos ambrotos, oude k’ Athēnē
tossēsd’ hysminēs ephepoi stoma kai poneoito·
sentences.l:
not even Ares, though he is a deathless god, nor Athena,
of so great a battle would go against the mouth, and toil at it;
sentences.i: not even Ares, deathless god though he is, nor Athena would go against the mouth of so great a battle and toil at it;
sentences.n: οὐδέ κ’ … οὐδέ κ’ ‘not even … nor’ goes with two optatives, ἐφέποι ‘would go against’ and πονέοιτο ‘would toil’, which are potential. ὅς περ θεὸς ἄμβροτος ‘though he is a deathless god’; ἄμβροτος ‘deathless’. τοσσῆσδ’ ὑσμίνης ‘of so great a battle’; στόμα ‘mouth’ is the front where the fighting is, as the mouth is the front of an animal.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅσσον μὲν ἐγὼ δύναμαι χερσίν τε ποσίν τε
καὶ σθένει, οὔ μ’ ἔτι φημὶ μεθησέμεν οὐδ’ ἠβαιόν,
ἀλλὰ μάλα στιχὸς εἶμι διαμπερές, οὐδέ τιν’ οἴω
Τρώων χαιρήσειν, ὅς τις σχεδὸν ἔγχεος ἔλθῃ.
sentences.tr:
all’ hosson men egō dynamai chersin te posin te
kai sthenei, ou m’ eti phēmi methēsemen oud’ ēbaion,
alla mala stichos eimi diamperes, oude tin’ oiō
Trōōn chairēsein, hos tis schedon encheos elthēi.
sentences.l:
but as much as I am able, with hands and feet
and strength, I say I shall not slacken any more, not even a little,
but greatly along the rank I shall go, right through, and I think not one
of the Trojans will rejoice, whoever comes near my spear.”
sentences.i: But as far as I am able, with hands and feet and strength, I say I shall not slack off any more, not the least bit, but I shall go clean through the line, and I think that none of the Trojans will rejoice, whoever comes near my spear.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅσσον μὲν ἐγὼ δύναμαι ‘but as far as I am able’, with χερσίν τε ποσίν τε ‘with hands and with feet’ and σθένει ‘strength’. οὔ μ’ ἔτι φημὶ μεθησέμεν οὐδ’ ἠβαιόν ‘I say I shall not slacken any more, not even a little’: μεθησέμεν is the epic future infinitive of μεθίημι ‘let go, slacken’. μάλα στιχὸς εἶμι διαμπερές ‘but I shall go clean through the line’: μάλα ‘greatly’ strengthens the phrase, στιχός is the genitive singular of στίξ (Attic στίχος) ‘rank, line’, giving the ground he crosses, and διαμπερές means ‘right through’. οἴω ‘I think’ (οἴομαι) takes Τρώων χαιρήσειν ‘that none of the Trojans will rejoice’; ὅς τις … ἔλθῃ ‘whoever comes’ is aorist subjunctive, and σχεδὸν ἔγχεος ‘near the spear’ takes the genitive. Achilles’ speech ends.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτ’ ἐποτρύνων· Τρώεσσι δὲ φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ
κέκλεθ’ ὁμοκλήσας, φάτο δ’ ἴμεναι ἄντ’ Ἀχιλῆος·
sentences.tr:
hōs phat’ epotrynōn· Trōessi de phaidimos Hektōr
kekleth’ homoklēsas, phato d’ imenai ant’ Achilēos·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, urging them on; and to the Trojans glorious Hector
called, shouting at them, and said he would go against Achilles:
sentences.i: So he spoke, urging them on; and glorious Hector called to the Trojans, shouting at them, and said that he would go against Achilles:
sentences.n: ὣς φάτ’ ἐποτρύνων ‘so he spoke, urging them on’: φάτ’ is the unaugmented aorist of φημί, ἐποτρύνων the present participle of ἐποτρύνω ‘urge on’. κέκλεθ’ is κέκλετο, a reduplicated aorist of κέλομαι ‘call to’, with the dative Τρώεσσι. φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ ‘glorious Hector’ is rendered so every time. ὁμοκλήσας is the aorist participle of ὁμοκλάω ‘shout at’. φάτο is the aorist middle of φημί, and ἴμεναι the epic infinitive of εἶμι; ἄντ’ (an elided ἄντα) takes the genitive, ‘against Achilles’.

sentences.t: Τρῶες ὑπέρθυμοι μὴ δείδιτε Πηλεΐωνα.
sentences.tr: Trōes hyperthymoi mē deidite Pēleïōna.
sentences.l: “High-hearted Trojans, do not fear the son of Peleus.
sentences.i: “High-hearted Trojans, do not fear the son of Peleus.
sentences.n: Τρῶες ὑπέρθυμοι ‘high-hearted Trojans’ (ὑπέρθυμος from ὑπέρ ‘over’ and θυμός ‘heart’). μὴ δείδιτε ‘do not fear’ is the imperative of δείδω; Πηλεΐωνα is the accusative of the patronymic Πηλεΐων ‘son of Peleus’, meaning Achilles.

sentences.t:
καί κεν ἐγὼ ἐπέεσσι καὶ ἀθανάτοισι μαχοίμην,
ἔγχεϊ δ’ ἀργαλέον, ἐπεὶ ἦ πολὺ φέρτεροί εἰσιν.
sentences.tr:
kai ken egō epeessi kai athanatoisi machoimēn,
encheï d’ argaleon, epei ē poly pherteroi eisin.
sentences.l:
Even I, with words, even with immortals could fight,
but with the spear it is hard, since truly they are much stronger.
sentences.i: I could fight even the immortals with words, but with the spear it is hard, since they are far stronger.
sentences.n: καί κεν ἐγώ … μαχοίμην ‘even I could fight’: κεν with the optative makes it potential. ἐπέεσσι ‘with words’, the epic dative plural of ἔπος; καὶ ἀθανάτοισι ‘even with immortals’. ἔγχεϊ δ’ ἀργαλέον ‘but with the spear it is hard’: ἐστί and the infinitive (‘to fight’) are left unsaid. ἐπεὶ ἦ πολὺ φέρτεροί εἰσιν ‘since truly they are far stronger’: φέρτεροι ‘stronger’, πολύ ‘far’ is adverbial.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ Ἀχιλεὺς πάντεσσι τέλος μύθοις ἐπιθήσει,
ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν τελέει, τὸ δὲ καὶ μεσσηγὺ κολούει.
sentences.tr:
oud’ Achileus pantessi telos mythois epithēsei,
alla to men teleei, to de kai messēgy kolouei.
sentences.l:
Nor will Achilles on all his words set fulfilment,
but one he will fulfil, and another even half-way cut short.
sentences.i: Nor will Achilles bring all his words to fulfilment; some he will fulfil, and others he will cut short half-way.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ Ἀχιλεὺς … τέλος … ἐπιθήσει ‘nor will Achilles put fulfilment on’, the future of ἐπιτίθημι; μύθοις is dative, with πάντεσσι, the epic dative plural of πᾶς. ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν τελέει, τὸ δὲ … κολούει ‘but one he will fulfil, another he will cut short’: τελέει is the uncontracted form of τελέω ‘fulfil’ (present or epic future) and κολούει the present of κολούω ‘cut short’; after the future ἐπιθήσει the English takes both as futures. μεσσηγύ ‘half-way’.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἐγὼ ἀντίος εἶμι καὶ εἰ πυρὶ χεῖρας ἔοικεν,
εἰ πυρὶ χεῖρας ἔοικε, μένος δ’ αἴθωνι σιδήρῳ.
sentences.tr:
tou d’ egō antios eimi kai ei pyri cheiras eoiken,
ei pyri cheiras eoike, menos d’ aithōni sidērōi.
sentences.l:
Against him I will go, even if in hands he is like fire,
if in hands he is like fire, and in might like fire-bright iron.”
sentences.i: I will go to meet him, even if his hands are like fire, if his hands are like fire and his might like fire-bright iron.”
sentences.n: τοῦ δ’ ἐγὼ ἀντίος εἶμι ‘I shall go against him’: τοῦ is ‘him’ (Achilles), ἀντίος ‘facing’, εἶμι ‘I shall go’. καὶ εἰ ‘even if’; πυρὶ χεῖρας ἔοικεν ‘he is like fire in his hands’: ἔοικεν ‘is like’ takes the dative πυρί, and χεῖρας is an accusative of respect. Line 372 repeats the clause and adds μένος … αἴθωνι σιδήρῳ ‘in might like fire-bright iron’: μένος ‘might’ is accusative of respect, αἴθων ‘fire-bright’ is from αἴθω ‘burn’ (a traditional gloss). Hector’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτ’ ἐποτρύνων, οἳ δ’ ἀντίοι ἔγχε’ ἄειραν
Τρῶες· τῶν δ’ ἄμυδις μίχθη μένος, ὦρτο δ’ ἀϋτή.
sentences.tr:
hōs phat’ epotrynōn, hoi d’ antioi enche’ aeiran
Trōes· tōn d’ amydis michthē menos, ōrto d’ aÿtē.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, urging them on, and they, facing the foe, raised their spears,
the Trojans; and of them together was mingled the might, and a battle-cry arose.
sentences.i: So he spoke, urging them on, and the Trojans raised their spears to face the foe; and the might of both sides was mingled together, and a battle-cry arose.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτ’ ἐποτρύνων is the same line-opening as at 364, now closing Hector’s speech. οἳ δ’ … Τρῶες ‘and they, the Trojans’; ἀντίοι ‘facing’; ἔγχε’ is ἔγχεα ‘spears’; ἄειραν is the aorist of ἀείρω ‘raised’. τῶν δ’ ἄμυδις μίχθη μένος ‘of them together the might was mingled’: τῶν is the two armies, ἄμυδις ‘together’, μίχθη the aorist passive of μίγνυμι. ὦρτο is a short aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘arose’; ἀϋτή ‘battle-cry’.

sentences.t: καὶ τότ’ ἄρ’ Ἕκτορα εἶπε παραστὰς Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.tr: kai tot’ ar’ Hektora eipe parastas Phoibos Apollōn·
sentences.l: And then indeed to Hector spoke, standing beside him, Phoebus Apollo:
sentences.i: And then Phoebus Apollo stood beside Hector and spoke:
sentences.n: καὶ τότ’ ἄρ’ ‘and then indeed’. Ἕκτορα εἶπε παραστάς ‘spoke to Hector, standing beside him’: εἶπε takes the accusative of the person spoken to, and παραστάς is the aorist participle of παρίστημι ‘stand beside’. Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων ‘Phoebus Apollo’ is the name rendered as it stands.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ μηκέτι πάμπαν Ἀχιλλῆϊ προμάχιζε,
ἀλλὰ κατὰ πληθύν τε καὶ ἐκ φλοίσβοιο δέδεξο,
μή πώς σ’ ἠὲ βάλῃ ἠὲ σχεδὸν ἄορι τύψῃ.
sentences.tr:
Hektor mēketi pampan Achillēï promachize,
alla kata plēthyn te kai ek phloisboio dedexo,
mē pōs s’ ēe balēi ēe schedon aori typsēi.
sentences.l:
“Hector, no longer at all against Achilles fight in front,
but among the crowd and out of the roar take your place,
lest somehow either he hit you, or near with a sword strike you.”
sentences.i: “Hector, do not go on fighting in the front rank against Achilles, but keep to the crowd, out of the roar of battle, lest he somehow hit you with a throw or strike you close at hand with his sword.”
sentences.n: μηκέτι πάμπαν ‘no longer at all’ goes with προμάχιζε, the imperative of προμαχίζω ‘fight in the front’; Ἀχιλλῆϊ is dative, ‘against Achilles’. κατὰ πληθύν ‘among the crowd’ (κατά with the accusative), ἐκ φλοίσβοιο ‘out of the roar’ (the din of battle). δέδεξο is a reduplicated imperative of δέχομαι; its exact sense here is not certain, and ‘take your place, hold to’ is a guess from δέχομαι ‘receive, take up’. μή πώς σ’ … ‘lest somehow … you’ takes two subjunctives with ἠέ … ἠέ ‘either … or’: βάλῃ ‘hit’ (with a thrown weapon) and τύψῃ ‘strike’; σχεδὸν ἄορι ‘close at hand, with a sword’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, Ἕκτωρ δ’ αὖτις ἐδύσετο οὐλαμὸν ἀνδρῶν
ταρβήσας, ὅτ’ ἄκουσε θεοῦ ὄπα φωνήσαντος.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, Hektōr d’ autis edyseto oulamon andrōn
tarbēsas, hot’ akouse theou opa phōnēsantos.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Hector back again plunged into the crowd of men,
terrified, when he heard the voice of the god speaking.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Hector plunged back into the crowd of men, terrified, when he heard the voice of the god speaking.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ ‘so he spoke’: ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο (from φημί) with its τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of Ἕκτωρ. αὖτις ‘back again’; ἐδύσετο is the aorist middle of δύω ‘enter, plunge into’, with the accusative οὐλαμὸν ἀνδρῶν ‘the crowd of men’ (οὐλαμός is a rare word). ταρβήσας ‘terrified’ is the aorist participle of ταρβέω. ὅτ’ ἄκουσε θεοῦ ὄπα φωνήσαντος ‘when he heard the voice of the god speaking’: ὄπα is the object, and the genitive participle φωνήσαντος agrees with θεοῦ.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ Ἀχιλεὺς Τρώεσσι θόρε φρεσὶν εἱμένος ἀλκὴν
σμερδαλέα ἰάχων, πρῶτον δ’ ἕλεν Ἰφιτίωνα
ἐσθλὸν Ὀτρυντεΐδην πολέων ἡγήτορα λαῶν,
sentences.tr:
en d’ Achileus Trōessi thore phresin heimenos alkēn
smerdalea iachōn, prōton d’ helen Iphitiōna
esthlon Otrynteïdēn poleōn hēgētora laōn,
sentences.l:
And in among the Trojans leapt Achilles, clothed in might in his wits,
terribly crying out, and first he took Iphition,
good son of Otrynteus, leader of many peoples,
sentences.i: Achilles leapt in among the Trojans, clothed in might in his wits, crying out terribly, and the first man he killed was Iphition, the good son of Otrynteus, leader of many peoples,
sentences.n: ἐν δ’ … θόρε ‘leapt in’ is ἐν and the aorist of θρῴσκω ‘leap’ split apart (tmesis), with the dative Τρώεσσι ‘among the Trojans’. φρεσὶν εἱμένος ἀλκήν ‘clothed in might in his wits’: εἱμένος is a perfect passive participle of ἕννυμι ‘clothe’, and ἀλκήν is the thing he is clothed in. σμερδαλέα ἰάχων ‘crying out terribly’. πρῶτον δ’ ἕλεν ‘and first he took’: ἕλεν is the aorist of αἱρέω, ‘took’, here ‘killed’. Ἰφιτίωνα and Ὀτρυντεΐδην ‘son of Otrynteus’ (a patronymic) are accusatives; ἐσθλόν ‘good’; πολέων ἡγήτορα λαῶν ‘leader of many peoples’, with πολέων the epic genitive plural of πολύς. The unit is cut at the comma because the sentence runs five lines.

sentences.t:
ὃν νύμφη τέκε νηῒς Ὀτρυντῆϊ πτολιπόρθῳ
Τμώλῳ ὕπο νιφόεντι Ὕδης ἐν πίονι δήμῳ·
sentences.tr:
hon nymphē teke nēïs Otryntēï ptoliporthōi
Tmōlōi hypo niphoenti Hydēs en pioni dēmōi·
sentences.l:
whom a nymph bore, a naiad, to Otrynteus, city-sacking,
beneath snowy Tmolus, in the rich land of Hyde;
sentences.i: whom a water-nymph bore to Otrynteus, sacker of cities, beneath snowy Tmolus, in the rich land of Hyde;
sentences.n: ὃν … τέκε ‘whom … bore’: τέκε is the aorist of τίκτω without augment. νύμφη νηΐς ‘a nymph, a naiad’: νύμφη is here a divine nymph, not a bride, and νηΐς is the water-nymph (naiad) kind. Ὀτρυντῆϊ πτολιπόρθῳ ‘to Otrynteus, sacker of cities’ (dative; πτολίπορθος ‘city-sacking’). Τμώλῳ ὕπο νιφόεντι ‘beneath snowy Tmolus’: ὕπο follows its noun and takes the dative; Tmolus is a mountain. Ὕδης ἐν πίονι δήμῳ ‘in the rich land of Hyde’, a place name.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἰθὺς μεμαῶτα βάλ’ ἔγχεϊ δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
μέσσην κὰκ κεφαλήν· ἣ δ’ ἄνδιχα πᾶσα κεάσθη,
δούπησεν δὲ πεσών, ὃ δ’ ἐπεύξατο δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ithys memaōta bal’ encheï dios Achilleus
messēn kak kephalēn· hē d’ andicha pasa keasthē,
doupēsen de pesōn, ho d’ epeuxato dios Achilleus·
sentences.l:
Him, straight at him, eager, struck with his spear heavenly Achilles
down on the middle of the head; and it all was split in two,
and he fell with a thud, and he vaunted, heavenly Achilles:
sentences.i: Heavenly Achilles struck him with his spear as he came on eagerly, straight at him, in the middle of the head, and it was split all in two; he fell with a thud, and heavenly Achilles cried out in triumph over him:
sentences.n: τὸν … μεμαῶτα ‘him, eager’: μεμαῶτα is the perfect participle of μέμαα ‘be eager’, and ἰθύς ‘straight at (him)’ goes with it; the free English makes him charge eagerly. βάλ’ is the aorist of βάλλω ‘struck’; ἔγχεϊ ‘with the spear’. μέσσην κὰκ κεφαλήν ‘down on the middle of the head’ (the free English says ‘in’): κὰκ is κατά with its last letter taken over by the κ that follows, and μέσσην agrees with κεφαλήν. ἣ δ’ ‘and it’ (the head); ἄνδιχα πᾶσα κεάσθη ‘was split all in two’, the aorist passive of κεάζω. δούπησεν δὲ πεσών ‘and he fell with a thud’. ἐπεύξατο ‘cried out in triumph’ is the aorist of ἐπεύχομαι, here of a taunt over the dead, not a prayer. δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς ‘heavenly Achilles’ is translated every time.

sentences.t: κεῖσαι Ὀτρυντεΐδη πάντων ἐκπαγλότατ’ ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.tr: keisai Otrynteïdē pantōn ekpaglotat’ andrōn·
sentences.l: “You lie, son of Otrynteus, most terrifying of all men;
sentences.i: “You lie there, son of Otrynteus, most terrifying of all men;
sentences.n: κεῖσαι ‘you lie’ is the second person singular of κεῖμαι. Ὀτρυντεΐδη is the vocative of the patronymic ‘son of Otrynteus’. πάντων ἐκπαγλότατ’ ἀνδρῶν ‘most terrifying of all men’: ἐκπαγλότατε is the superlative of ἔκπαγλος ‘terrifying’, and the phrase is mockery of a dead man.

sentences.t:
ἐνθάδε τοι θάνατος, γενεὴ δέ τοί ἐστ’ ἐπὶ λίμνῃ
Γυγαίῃ, ὅθι τοι τέμενος πατρώϊόν ἐστιν
Ὕλλῳ ἐπ’ ἰχθυόεντι καὶ Ἕρμῳ δινήεντι.
sentences.tr:
enthade toi thanatos, geneē de toi est’ epi limnēi
Gygaiēi, hothi toi temenos patrōïon estin
Hyllōi ep’ ichthyoenti kai Hermōi dinēenti.
sentences.l:
here for you is death, and your lineage is by the lake
Gygaean, where for you is your father’s precinct
by fish-teeming Hyllus and eddying Hermus.”
sentences.i: Here is your death, but your family has its place by the Gygaean lake, where your father’s estate lies, by fish-teeming Hyllus and eddying Hermus.”
sentences.n: ἐνθάδε τοι θάνατος ‘here for you is death’: τοι is the enclitic dative of σύ, and ἐστί is left out. γενεὴ δέ τοί ἐστ’ ἐπὶ λίμνῃ Γυγαίῃ ‘but your lineage is by the Gygaean lake’: γενεή ‘lineage’ here means the place where his kin belong, and Γυγαίῃ ‘Gygaean’ is an adjective made from a name. ὅθι ‘where’; τέμενος πατρώϊον ‘your father’s precinct’, land set apart (πατρώϊος ‘of the father’). Ὕλλῳ ἐπ’ ἰχθυόεντι καὶ Ἕρμῳ δινήεντι ‘by fish-teeming Hyllus and eddying Hermus’: ἐπί takes the dative, two river names; ἰχθυόεις ‘teeming with fish’ (ἰχθύς), δινήεις ‘eddying’ (δίνη ‘eddy’). Achilles’ taunt ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος, τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψε.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’ euchomenos, ton de skotos osse kalypse.
sentences.l: So he spoke, declaring, and darkness covered his two eyes.
sentences.i: So he declared aloud, and darkness covered his eyes.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος ‘so he spoke, declaring’: εὔχομαι here means ‘declare, claim’ in a vaunt, not ‘pray’. τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψε is the death formula: τόν is the man, ὄσσε the dual ‘two eyes’ (the part struck), κάλυψε the unaugmented aorist of καλύπτω. The paragraph break follows the taunt.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν Ἀχαιῶν ἵπποι ἐπισσώτροις δατέοντο
πρώτῃ ἐν ὑσμίνῃ·
sentences.tr:
ton men Achaiōn hippoi epissōtrois dateonto
prōtēi en hysminēi·
sentences.l:
Him, on the one hand, the horses of the Achaeans with their tires were dividing
in the first battle;
sentences.i: The horses of the Achaeans were dividing him up with their tires in the foremost fighting;
sentences.n: τὸν μέν ‘him, for his part’; Ἀχαιῶν ἵπποι ‘the horses of the Achaeans’. ἐπισσώτροις ‘with their tires’: ἐπίσσωτρον is the rim of a wheel, so the chariots the horses draw tear the body up. δατέοντο is the imperfect of δατέομαι ‘divide, cut up’. πρώτῃ ἐν ὑσμίνῃ ‘in the first (foremost) battle’; ὑσμίνη ‘battle’. The ano teleia ends the unit in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ Δημολέοντα
ἐσθλὸν ἀλεξητῆρα μάχης Ἀντήνορος υἱὸν
νύξε κατὰ κρόταφον, κυνέης διὰ χαλκοπαρῄου.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ep’ autōi Dēmoleonta
esthlon alexētēra machēs Antēnoros huion
nyxe kata krotaphon, kyneēs dia chalkoparēiou.
sentences.l:
and he, after him, Demoleon,
good warder-off of battle, Antenor’s son,
stabbed at the temple, through the bronze-cheeked helmet.
sentences.i: And next he stabbed Demoleon, the good defender in battle, son of Antenor, at the temple, through the bronze-cheeked helmet.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ‘and he, next after him’ (Achilles). Δημολέοντα ‘Demoleon’; ἐσθλὸν ἀλεξητῆρα μάχης ‘a good defender in battle’: ἀλεξητήρ is a ‘warder-off’, from ἀλέξω ‘ward off’, with the genitive μάχης. Ἀντήνορος υἱόν ‘son of Antenor’. νύξε is the aorist of νύσσω ‘stab’; κατὰ κρόταφον ‘at the temple’. κυνέης διὰ χαλκοπαρῄου ‘through the bronze-cheeked helmet’: χαλκοπαρῄου is a two-ending adjective, probably for the bronze cheek-pieces.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα χαλκείη κόρυς ἔσχεθεν, ἀλλὰ δι’ αὐτῆς
αἰχμὴ ἱεμένη ῥῆξ’ ὀστέον, ἐγκέφαλος δὲ
ἔνδον ἅπας πεπάλακτο·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ara chalkeiē korys eschethen, alla di’ autēs
aichmē hiemenē rhēx’ osteon, enkephalos de
endon hapas pepalakto·
sentences.i: The bronze helmet did not hold, but the spear-point, driving on through it, broke the bone, and all the brain within was spattered;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἄρα χαλκείη κόρυς ἔσχεθεν ‘and the bronze helmet did not hold’: χαλκείη is ‘of bronze’, and ἔσχεθεν is the aorist of ἔχω, here without an object, ‘held firm’. ἀλλὰ δι’ αὐτῆς … ῥῆξ’ ὀστέον ‘but through it … broke the bone’: δι’ αὐτῆς is ‘through it’ (the helmet), ῥῆξ’ the aorist of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’, and ἱεμένη ‘driving on’ the present participle of ἵεμαι, agreeing with αἰχμή ‘spear-point’. ἐγκέφαλος ‘brain’; ἔνδον ἅπας ‘all within’; πεπάλακτο is the pluperfect passive of παλάσσω ‘spatter’.

sentences.t: δάμασσε δέ μιν μεμαῶτα.
sentences.tr: damasse de min memaōta.
sentences.l: and he subdued him, eager as he was.
sentences.i: and so he overcame him as he charged.
sentences.n: δάμασσε is the aorist of δαμάζω ‘subdue, overcome’, without augment, with μιν ‘him’. μεμαῶτα is the perfect participle of μέμαα ‘be eager’, agreeing with μιν: Demoleon was eager (the Greek does not say for what) when Achilles overcame him. Achilles is the unnamed subject.

sentences.t:
Ἱπποδάμαντα δ’ ἔπειτα καθ’ ἵππων ἀΐξαντα
πρόσθεν ἕθεν φεύγοντα μετάφρενον οὔτασε δουρί.
sentences.tr:
Hippodamanta d’ epeita kath’ hippōn aïxanta
prosthen hethen pheugonta metaphrenon outase douri.
sentences.l:
And Hippodamas then, down from the horses darting,
before him fleeing, in the back he wounded with his spear.
sentences.i: And then he wounded Hippodamas in the back with his spear, as he darted down from his horses and fled before him.
sentences.n: Ἱπποδάμαντα ‘Hippodamas’ is the accusative; the name is ἵππος ‘horse’ and δάμνημι ‘tame’. καθ’ ἵππων ἀΐξαντα ‘darting down from the horses’: κατά takes the genitive ‘down from’, and ἀΐξαντα is the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’. πρόσθεν ἕθεν φεύγοντα ‘fleeing before him’: ἕθεν is the epic genitive of the third-person pronoun, here Achilles, with πρόσθεν ‘in front of’. μετάφρενον οὔτασε δουρί ‘wounded in the back with his spear’: μετάφρενον is the back between the shoulders, accusative of the part; οὔτασε is the aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound’; δουρί is the epic dative of δόρυ ‘spear’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ θυμὸν ἄϊσθε καὶ ἤρυγεν, ὡς ὅτε ταῦρος
ἤρυγεν ἑλκόμενος Ἑλικώνιον ἀμφὶ ἄνακτα
κούρων ἑλκόντων· γάνυται δέ τε τοῖς ἐνοσίχθων·
sentences.tr:
autar ho thymon aïsthe kai ērygen, hōs hote tauros
ērygen helkomenos Helikōnion amphi anakta
kourōn helkontōn· ganytai de te tois enosichthōn·
sentences.i: But he gasped out his life and bellowed, as a bull bellows when it is dragged about the Heliconian lord by youths who drag it, and the earth-shaker is delighted with them;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ ‘but he’ is Hippodamas. θυμὸν ἄϊσθε ‘gasped out his life’: ἄϊσθε is the aorist of ἀΐσθω ‘gasp out’, a rare verb whose origin is not known. ἤρυγεν is the aorist of ἐρεύγομαι ‘bellow’. A simile follows: ὡς ὅτε ταῦρος ‘as when a bull’; ἑλκόμενος ‘being dragged’ (present passive participle), κούρων ἑλκόντων ‘by youths dragging’ (a genitive absolute). Ἑλικώνιον … ἄνακτα ‘the Heliconian lord’ is usually taken as Poseidon, since ἐνοσίχθων closes the line as the one pleased; where the epithet comes from (the town Helice or the mountain Helicon) is not certain. γάνυται ‘is delighted’; τε is the epic particle of a general truth; τοῖς ‘with them’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα τόν γ’ ἐρυγόντα λίπ’ ὀστέα θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ·
sentences.tr: hōs ara ton g’ erygonta lip’ ostea thymos agēnōr·
sentences.l: So then, as he bellowed, left his bones the manly spirit;
sentences.i: So, as he bellowed, the proud spirit left his bones;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα ‘so then’ closes the simile. τόν γ’ ἐρυγόντα ‘him as he bellowed’ is the aorist participle of ἐρεύγομαι, the verb of ἤρυγεν. λίπ’ ὀστέα ‘left his bones’: λίπ’ is the aorist of λείπω without augment, and τόν and ὀστέα are the man and the part he is left. θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ ‘the manly spirit’ (i ‘the proud spirit’): ἀγήνωρ is ‘manly’ in the literal English and ‘proud’ in the free English each time.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ βῆ σὺν δουρὶ μετ’ ἀντίθεον Πολύδωρον
Πριαμίδην.
sentences.tr:
autar ho bē syn douri met’ antitheon Polydōron
Priamidēn.
sentences.l:
But he went with his spear after godlike Polydorus,
son of Priam.
sentences.i: But he went with his spear after godlike Polydorus, son of Priam.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ βῆ ‘but he set out’ (Achilles), βῆ the aorist of βαίνω without augment. σὺν δουρί ‘with his spear’. μετ’ ἀντίθεον Πολύδωρον ‘after godlike Polydorus’: μετά with the accusative means ‘in pursuit of’; ἀντίθεος ‘godlike’. Πριαμίδην ‘son of Priam’ is a patronymic. The sentence ends here in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ οὔ τι πατὴρ εἴασκε μάχεσθαι,
οὕνεκά οἱ μετὰ παισὶ νεώτατος ἔσκε γόνοιο,
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ou ti patēr eiaske machesthai,
houneka hoi meta paisi neōtatos eske gonoio,
sentences.l:
And him not at all would his father allow to fight,
because among his children youngest in birth he was,
sentences.i: His father would not let him fight at all, because he was the youngest of his children in birth,
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ οὔ τι πατὴρ εἴασκε μάχεσθαι ‘and his father would not at all let him fight’: εἴασκε is the iterative imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’, with the suffix -σκ- marking something done again and again; the father is Priam. οὕνεκά οἱ ‘because to him’; μετὰ παισί ‘among the children’; νεώτατος ἔσκε γόνοιο ‘he was the youngest in birth’: ἔσκε is the iterative of εἰμί, and γόνοιο is the epic genitive of γόνος ‘offspring, birth’. The unit is cut at the comma because the sentence runs five lines.

sentences.t:
καί οἱ φίλτατος ἔσκε, πόδεσσι δὲ πάντας ἐνίκα
δὴ τότε νηπιέῃσι ποδῶν ἀρετὴν ἀναφαίνων
θῦνε διὰ προμάχων, εἷος φίλον ὤλεσε θυμόν.
sentences.tr:
kai hoi philtatos eske, podessi de pantas enika
dē tote nēpieēisi podōn aretēn anaphainōn
thyne dia promachōn, heios philon ōlese thymon.
sentences.i: and he was dearest to him, and in speed of foot beat them all; so then, in his childish ways, displaying the excellence of his feet, he rushed through the foremost fighters until he lost his life.
sentences.n: καί οἱ φίλτατος ἔσκε ‘and he was dearest to him’ (ἔσκε again iterative); πόδεσσι δὲ πάντας ἐνίκα ‘and in his feet he beat them all’, with πόδεσσι the epic dative plural and ἐνίκα the imperfect of νικάω. δὴ τότε ‘so then’; νηπιέῃσι ‘in childish ways’ is the dative plural of νηπιέη, from νήπιος ‘child’; ποδῶν ἀρετήν ‘the excellence of his feet’, that is, his speed; ἀναφαίνων ‘displaying’. θῦνε διὰ προμάχων ‘rushed through the front-fighters’: θῦνε is the imperfect of θύνω, and διὰ προμάχων ‘through the foremost fighters’. εἷος is ‘until’ (= ἕως); φίλον ὤλεσε θυμόν ‘lost his dear life’ (aorist of ὄλλυμι).

sentences.t:
τὸν βάλε μέσσον ἄκοντι ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
νῶτα παραΐσσοντος, ὅθι ζωστῆρος ὀχῆες
χρύσειοι σύνεχον καὶ διπλόος ἤντετο θώρηξ·
sentences.tr:
ton bale messon akonti podarkēs dios Achilleus
nōta paraïssontos, hothi zōstēros ochēes
chryseioi synechon kai diploos ēnteto thōrēx·
sentences.i: Swift-footed, heavenly Achilles struck him in the middle with a javelin, in the back as he darted past, in the place where the golden clasps of the belt held fast and the double breastplate met them;
sentences.n: τὸν βάλε … ἄκοντι ‘struck him … with a javelin’ (ἄκων ‘javelin’). μέσσον ‘in the middle’ and νῶτα ‘in the back’ both name the place struck; νῶτα παραΐσσοντος ‘in the back as he darted past’: the participle (παραΐσσω ‘dart past’) is genitive, as if ‘him darting past’. ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς ‘swift-footed, heavenly Achilles’: ποδάρκης is a stock epithet whose formation is uncertain (probably πούς + ἀρκέω), translated every time and kept apart from ποδώκης ‘fleet-footed’. ὅθι ‘where’; ζωστῆρος ὀχῆες χρύσειοι ‘the golden clasps of the belt’; σύνεχον is the imperfect of συνέχω ‘hold together’; διπλόος θώρηξ ‘the double breastplate’ (θώρηξ = θώραξ); ἤντετο is the imperfect of ἀντάω ‘meet’.

sentences.t:
ἀντικρὺ δὲ διέσχε παρ’ ὀμφαλὸν ἔγχεος αἰχμή,
γνὺξ δ’ ἔριπ’ οἰμώξας, νεφέλη δέ μιν ἀμφεκάλυψε
κυανέη, προτὶ οἷ δ’ ἔλαβ’ ἔντερα χερσὶ λιασθείς.
sentences.tr:
antikry de diesche par’ omphalon encheos aichmē,
gnyx d’ erip’ oimōxas, nephelē de min amphekalypse
kyaneē, proti hoi d’ elab’ entera chersi liastheis.
sentences.l:
and straight through, beside the navel, passed the point of the spear,
and on his knees he crashed down, wailing, and a cloud covered him about,
dark, and toward himself he took his entrails in his hands, bending down.
sentences.i: The spear’s point passed straight through beside his navel, and he crashed down on his knees, wailing, and a dark cloud closed over him, and as he sank down he took his entrails to himself in his hands.
sentences.n: ἀντικρύ ‘straight through’; διέσχε is the aorist of διέχω ‘pass through’; παρ’ ὀμφαλόν ‘beside the navel’. ἔγχεος αἰχμή ‘the point of the spear’ is the subject, held to the end of the line. γνὺξ δ’ ἔριπ’ οἰμώξας ‘and on his knees he crashed down, wailing’: ἔριπε is the aorist of ἐρείπω ‘crash down’, οἰμώξας the aorist participle of οἰμώζω ‘wail’. νεφέλη … κυανέη ‘a dark cloud’, with μιν ἀμφεκάλυψε ‘covered him about’ (aorist). προτὶ οἷ … ἔλαβ’ ἔντερα χερσὶ λιασθείς ‘and toward himself he took his entrails in his hands, bending down’: προτί is πρός, οἷ ‘to himself’, ἔντερα ‘entrails’, and λιασθείς is the aorist passive participle of λιάζομαι ‘bend down’ (i ‘sank down’).
